newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian markets surge on foreign buying.
newsitem.headline: Russian markets surge on foreign buying.

text.p: Russian financial markets surged on Wednesday on heavy foreign investment in Treasury bills and shares amid near euphoria about Russia's economic prospects.
Investors shrugged off worries about President Boris Yeltsin's health and political in-fighting in the Kremlin to drive T-bill yields to a record low and push up shares on record trading volumes.

"I can now see very big buying money," said United City Bank equities trader Samit Yakovlev. "And it is not the money of former clients, but new money as well. And each new price spiral stimulates investors more and more, as they are afraid to miss the boat."
Volumes on the Russian Trading System, the electronic share market similar to NASDAQ in the U.S., hit a record $46.97 million, as the RTS index of 24 shares rose 6.91 percent to 181.64.
The index is still off the July 4 high of 227.79 which it touched after Yeltsin was re-elected, but dealers said, those levels were now within reach again.
At an auction of six-month Treasury bills, the average yield fell to a record low 49.63 percent.
Bids totalled a massive 15.92 trillion roubles ($2.94 billion) for the 10 trillion roubles of paper on offer.
Central bank first deputy chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told Reuters that buying by foreigners was a major reason why yields had fallen below 50 percent for the first time.
He forecast yields would fall further as non-residents took advantage of a central bank scheme for them to invest in Russia.
"Our talks show that the process of non-residents coming in will continue at the same stormy rate, and the yield will fall," he said.
Non-residents had made bids of "several hundreds of millions of dollars" on Wednesday, he said.
Dealers said prices were rising on a combination of factors.
* International rating agencies awarded Russia better than expected credit ratings on Monday
* Yeltsin, preparing for heart surgery, moved from hospital to a sanatorium where aides say he is working and in satisfactory condition
* One of Russia's biggest companies, gas monopoly Gazprom, announced terms of an international share issue

The decision by the International Monetary Fund to pay out a another $350 million tranche under Russia's $10 billion loan programme, announced on Wednesday after Russian markets had closed, is likely to boost prices further.

"Everything coincided very favourably -- both ratings and price levels and the news about Gazprom and the information about Boris Yeltsin's preparation for the operation," said Andrei Galperin, a trader from Creditanstalt-Grant.
A flurry of rumours on international markets that Yeltsin was dead came too late to affect trading in Moscow.
Yeltsin's press office, clearly irritated by the rumours, said Yeltsin was working at the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow.
$1 = 5,420 roubles
